chapter.title: Plato and Aristotle: is the real world the one we see?

cards.body: Aristotle sat in Plato's school for about 20 years, then walked out disagreeing with his teacher about whether the table between them was fully real. At the long dinner-table argument, this is the first big split: Plato says **the real thing is the perfect pattern behind what you see**, and Aristotle answers that the real thing is right there, and you learn it by looking closely. Every guest since has had to pick a chair on one side or the other.

cards.prompt: Plato's famous story: prisoners chained in a cave since birth, facing a wall. A fire behind them throws shadows of puppets onto the wall. What do the prisoners think the shadows are?

options.text: A trick they have learned to ignore.
The real things, because shadows are all they have ever seen.

whyNot.a: That's the freed prisoner's view, not theirs: they have never seen anything else, so there is nothing to compare the shadows with.
whyNot.c: That's the end of the story, not the start: nobody in the cave knows there is an outside, let alone a sun.

cards.reteach: Plato's point is about us. We take the things in front of us to be the whole of reality, the way the prisoners take the shadows. The cave is a picture of being sure about something you have only ever seen one way.

cards.title: The cave, in 3 sentences
cards.body:
Here is the cave story from Plato's Republic. Prisoners chained since birth face a wall, and shadows of puppets thrown by a fire are the only things they have ever seen. One is freed, climbs into daylight, sees the sun, and comes back to tell the rest, who decide he has lost his mind.

Now the key. The shadows are ordinary things. The sun is a *form*, Plato's word for the perfect pattern a thing copies. Draw 100 circles and every one wobbles, yet you know exactly what a perfect circle is, though you have never seen one.

For Plato the real world is the one behind the one you see, **reached by thinking, not by looking**.

cards.title: A knife and a bucket
cards.body: After Plato died, Aristotle left Athens and ended up on the island of Lesbos, spending his days at a lagoon with a knife and a bucket. He cut open fish and wrote down what he found, including a small shark whose unborn young are joined to the mother by a cord, the way a mammal's are. Readers for centuries filed that under tall tales. In the 1840s a German biologist opened the same kind of shark and found the cord exactly as described. Plato wanted the perfect idea of a fish; Aristotle wanted **the fish, opened, on the table**.

cards.prompt: Two friends want to know what makes a bridge strong. Sam says: work out the perfect bridge in your head first; any built bridge is only a rough copy. Jo says: go and look at 50 bridges and see what the ones still standing share. Which chair is which?

options.text: Sam is Plato, Jo is Aristotle.
Sam is Aristotle, Jo is Plato.
Both are Plato: Jo is still hunting for the perfect bridge.

whyNot.b: That's the two swapped: Aristotle is the one with the knife and the bucket, learning by looking at many cases.
whyNot.c: That's Plato's goal pasted onto Aristotle's method: Jo never leaves the real bridges, which is exactly Aristotle's point.

cards.reteach: Ask one question: where does the truth live? If it lives in a perfect pattern you reach by thinking, that's Plato. If it lives in the things themselves and you reach it by looking at many of them, that's Aristotle.

cards.title: Aristotle's reply, and the catch
cards.body:
Aristotle's reply, after 20 years of listening: yes, there is a pattern, but it lives in the things. The pattern 'dog' lives in dogs. Take away every dog and it goes too. You find it by gathering many cases and noticing what repeats, which is the habit that grew into science.

You'd think that settled it 2,300 years ago. It didn't. A physicist writing an equation is trusting a clean pattern that no messy measurement will ever quite match, which is a very Platonic thing to do.

So where does a scientist sit? **Closer to Aristotle**, because the test is always 'go and look', with one foot under Plato's side of the table.

Dev, at a pub quiz, says: 'Plato thought this pint was an illusion.' Not quite: Plato never called the world fake, only a *copy*, real the way a photo of your mother is real and less real the way the photo is not her. Spot the slip by asking which they mean, fake like a forged note or a copy like a photo. Plato meant the photo.

cards.prompt: A painter shows the two men walking side by side. One points a finger at the sky. The other holds his palm flat, toward the ground. From this chapter, who is who?

options.text: Plato points up, Aristotle holds his palm down: the pattern behind things versus the things here.
Aristotle points up, Plato holds his palm down.
Both point up; they only disagreed about politics.

whyNot.b: That's the gestures swapped: Aristotle is the one who stays with the fish on the table, so the flat palm toward the ground is his.
whyNot.c: That's the one thing they shared, teacher and student, pasted over the one thing they split on: where the real lives.

cards.reteach: Up means 'the real pattern sits behind and above what you see', which is Plato's cave and sun. Down means 'the real is here, look at it', which is Aristotle's lagoon. The gesture is the whole argument.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Plato says the things you see are wobbly copies of perfect patterns, and the patterns are the real world, reached by thinking. Aristotle, his student for 20 years, answers that **the patterns live inside the things themselves**, so you learn the real by looking closely at many of them, which is why a scientist sits closer to his chair.

Tomorrow: in 1641 a man doubts everything, and finds exactly one thing he can't.
Tonight, draw 5 circles by hand. Look at the wobbles. Ask: how do you know what a perfect circle is when you have never seen one? That's Plato's question.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now tell the cave story in 3 sentences and say which chair, Plato's or Aristotle's, a scientist sits closer to.
